newsitem.title: FRANCE: Dress threatens jacket's extinction at Paris shows.
newsitem.headline: Dress threatens jacket's extinction at Paris shows.

text.p: - The dress was the winner of Paris' Spring-Summer season, challenging the separates concept that has long dominated women's wardrobes and sending a wave of femininity down the runway.
"The dress is the "must have' of this season. Last season was all about pants," said Joan Kaner of the U.S. department store Neiman Marcus.
But the suit jacket, the backbone of women's dressing, hovered on the brink of extinction as designers replaced them with lacy blouses or fluid cardigans.
"The return of dresses, with an emphasis on femininity and glamour will give women a reason to buy clothes this year," said Dawn Mello, president of Bergdorf Goodman.
"But we didn't see enough clothes for women to wear to work -- not enough suits and suiting, and a lack of jackets. Women wear jackets, they need them," she added.
Joseph Boitano, also of Bergdorf Goodman called it a "very strong" season but lamented the lack of mix-and-match separates that multiply a woman's options.

"We find that our customer looks for more separate dressing -- pants, skirts, jackets -- and we might have seen more of that," Boitano said. "It's something the Americans are doing a lot of and extremely well. They understand sportswear so well."

Valentino substituted the jacket by putting tiny sweaters, just long enough to cover the breasts, over lace blouses while Jean-Paul Gaultier made jackets part of all-in-one trompe l'oeil three-piece suits.

Chiffon, ruffles and lace dominated the catwalk, where daywear took a back seat to more abundant and well-worked evening clothes. Viscose knits or slink jerseys were also very popular, but fell flat when used for evening.
The dress was softly tailored, featuring several options -- asymetric hems, off-the-shoulder necklines and ruffled edges.
Another choice was in trousers, which were most often wide, replacing skinny cigarette slacks. They were best when married with blouses of lace or soft chiffon.

"It's been an interesting season. There seem to be two directions, one very soft and one very hard," Kaner said. "Some designers...mixed the two, putting a pair of men's grey trousers with a luscious chiffon blouse. I think women will understand it best that way."

The collections were also marked by an evolution in layering, with designers putting fluid, sheer tunics over trousers, transparent dresses over knickers and shorts, or simply sending models out topless -- as at Christian Dior and Dice Kayek.
Still other designers had their models wear only bikini bottoms under blouses.

"I think it's a good season. Everyone is so worried about the sheer fabrics and all the lingerie, but there are still a lot of good sellable clothes for our customers," said Nicole Fischelis of Saks Fifth Avenue. "Its a matter of editing."
Mello seemed more concerned. "Transparency needs layering. Women don't want to buy it without an underpinning, especially not at these expensive prices," she said.
"It depends on the designer. Valentino has a way of handling transparency so we know that when the clothes arrive in the store they are eminently wearable," she added.
Colour remained in full force, especially lavender and purple, but also pale yellow and green, chocolate and caramel.
"The continuation of colour is fantastic. Our customers love colour so we're very happy about that," Fischelis said.
